title: Level AA Is the Target, Not the Finish Line: What WCAG Conformance Actually Means
description: The four WCAG principles, the three levels, and what a conformance claim covers — a page, a process, and nothing beyond what's stated.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the four WCAG principles and the difference between Levels A, AA, and AAA
Determine what a WCAG conformance claim does and does not cover for a page versus a multi-step process

contentSections.body: Havenmark's project sponsor — a mid-size EU retailer selling homeware and electronics — kicks off the engagement with a one-line brief: "We need to be WCAG compliant before the deadline." That sentence sounds like a clear instruction. It's actually three unanswered questions stacked on top of each other: compliant with which level of WCAG, compliant on which pages, and what does "compliant" even mean for a site where a customer has to get through five separate screens — cart, address, shipping method, payment, confirmation — before a purchase actually completes. Before your team runs a single test, you have to be able to answer all three, in writing, or the audit has no defined finish line.

WCAG 2.2 organizes every success criterion under four principles, usually abbreviated **POUR**:

- **Perceivable** — information and interface components have to be presentable to users in ways they can actually perceive, not just ways that are technically encoded somewhere in the markup.
- **Operable** — interface components and navigation have to be operable, including from a keyboard alone, and without requiring interactions some users physically cannot perform.
- **Understandable** — information and interface behavior have to be understandable: predictable, with clear labels and clear error handling.
- **Robust** — content has to be robust enough to be interpreted reliably by a wide range of user agents, including assistive technologies, including ones that don't exist yet.

Every one of the ten success criteria this domain covers sits under one of those four.

Each criterion also carries a **level** — A, AA, or AAA — which is a statement about how severe the barrier is if the criterion fails, not about how hard the criterion is to implement. **Level A** covers the failures that block access outright for some group of users. **Level AA** covers failures that create serious difficulty even where access isn't strictly impossible — inadequate contrast, missing focus indicators, targets too small to hit reliably. **Level AAA** is the highest level, and WCAG's own conformance guidance is explicit that it does *not* recommend requiring AAA conformance as a general policy for an entire site: some AAA criteria genuinely can't be satisfied by every kind of content (a strict sign-language-interpretation requirement, for instance, isn't achievable for a live datafeed), so a blanket AAA requirement sets a target nobody can actually hit. Practically, and legally across the EU, **Level AA — meaning every Level A and every Level AA criterion — is the target.** Nobody scopes an EU accessibility audit against AAA.

One more piece of the standard worth knowing before it comes up in a client conversation: WCAG 2.2 actually *removed* a criterion that existed in 2.1 — 4.1.1 Parsing, which required well-formed markup (no duplicate IDs, properly nested tags). It was dropped because modern browsers and assistive technologies handle malformed markup consistently enough that the criterion stopped catching real problems. The standard evolves in both directions — new criteria get added, and criteria that stop being useful get retired.

contentSections.question: Before you read the next section: which level do EU law and most client contracts actually reference as the compliance bar — A, AA, or AAA?
contentSections.answer: AA — specifically every Level A and Level AA success criterion together. AAA is treated by WCAG's own conformance requirements as unsuitable to require site-wide, and no EU accessibility law or standard sets AAA as its baseline. If a client says "WCAG compliant" with no level named, AA is the level to confirm in writing before scoping anything.
contentSections.hint: Think about why WCAG itself advises against requiring its own top level as a blanket policy.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's product page passes every Level A and AA success criterion the agency tested. Its checkout is three steps: cart, shipping address, payment. Step 2 — the shipping address form — has one required field with no accessible label, which fails 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A). Steps 1 and 3 pass cleanly.
contentSections.question: Does the clean product-page report mean Havenmark's checkout process conforms at Level AA?

options.label: No — conformance applies to full pages and complete processes; one failing step breaks the whole process's conformance claim
Yes — two of the three steps pass, and a majority-passing process can still claim conformance
It depends on whether the failing field is Level A or Level AA — a Level AA-only failure wouldn't break the claim

feedback.process-fails: Correct. WCAG's conformance requirements extend a claim to complete processes as well as individual pages — a sequence like cart → address → payment → confirmation has to conform end to end, because a customer can't complete a purchase by stopping at the page that passed. One unlabeled required field on step 2 means the process does not conform at AA, regardless of how clean the product page or the other two checkout steps are.
feedback.mostly-passes: There's no such thing as a majority-passing conformance claim. Conformance isn't measured as a percentage of steps or criteria passed — it's every applicable criterion, met, across every page and process in scope. Two out of three steps passing is a two-thirds-failing process, not a passing one, for the purpose of an AA claim.
feedback.level-matters: The level of the specific failing criterion isn't what determines whether the process conforms — an AA claim requires every Level A *and* every Level AA criterion to be met. A Level A failure like this one breaks an AA claim exactly as thoroughly as a Level AA failure would; there's no tier of severity within "fails to conform" based on which level the broken criterion belongs to.

contentSections.concept: A conformance claim covers what it says it covers — full pages, and complete processes where a task requires more than one page to finish. The practical consequence: scoping "the checkout" means every step in that checkout has to be tested, and a single broken step anywhere in the sequence is enough to say the process doesn't conform, even when the surrounding pages look excellent.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's marketing team drafts a line for the company's investor update: "Our site is WCAG 2.2 AA conformant." Before that sentence goes out, it's worth being precise about what a claim like that actually asserts — and what it doesn't.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that's true about what a WCAG 2.2 AA conformance claim covers.

items.label: The claim should state exactly which pages and processes it covers — it doesn't have to mean the entire site by default
A 95% pass rate on an automated scan is close enough to justify claiming AA conformance
Every applicable Level A and AA criterion has to be met — there's no partial credit within a claimed level
A conformant page guarantees no user will ever encounter a barrier on it
A page can conform at AA and still have real usability problems that no WCAG success criterion happens to cover
For a multi-step process, every step has to conform — not just the page where the process begins

explanation.scope-stated: True. WCAG's own conformance requirements call for the claim to name the pages and processes it covers. "Conformant" with no stated scope invites exactly the wrong reading — that it means the whole site — and a marketing line that omits scope is making a bigger promise than the audit actually tested.
explanation.pass-rate: False. Conformance isn't a percentage. An automated scanner reporting 95% clean isn't measuring conformance at all — it's measuring how many of the checks it's capable of running came back clean, which is a different and much smaller thing than every applicable success criterion being met.
explanation.zero-exceptions: True. A claimed level requires every criterion at that level and every level below it. There's no WCAG mechanism for "mostly AA" — a page either meets a level's full requirement set or it doesn't, and a memo or statement that hedges with "largely conformant" is describing something WCAG has no name for.
explanation.guarantees-barrier-free: False, and a genuinely dangerous line to let stand in an investor update. WCAG's own success criteria don't claim to cover every possible usability problem — a conformant page can still be confusing, exhausting, or hostile to a specific disability in ways no criterion happens to test for.
explanation.coverage-gaps: True — and it's the honest version of the previous point. WCAG is a floor with known gaps, not a ceiling. Treating an AA claim as "we're done" rather than "we've cleared the documented minimum" is a common and avoidable overstatement.
explanation.process-all-steps: True, and it's the point from the checkout example: a claim covering "the store" without naming the checkout process specifically leaves ambiguous whether all three steps were actually tested, which is exactly the ambiguity a scoping memo exists to remove.

contentSections.synthesis: Four of the six hold up, and the two that don't share a pattern: both treat conformance as a measurement of how close something got, rather than as a binary statement about a defined, named scope. The corrected line for Havenmark's investor update isn't "our site is WCAG 2.2 AA conformant" — it's "[named pages and the checkout process, as of this date] conform to WCAG 2.2 Level AA," which is a claim someone can actually verify.

contentSections.body: Level AA — all of Level A and all of Level AA — is the practical and legal target; AAA isn't something you scope an EU audit against. A conformance claim covers exactly what it names: full pages, complete multi-step processes end to end, and nothing wider than that. "Compliant" with no level and no stated scope isn't a claim you can defend — it's a sentence waiting to become a dispute.

title: Five Criteria, Part One: What an Attribute Being Present Doesn't Tell You
description: 1.1.1, 1.3.1, 1.4.3, 1.4.11, and 2.1.1 — the criteria that generate real findings, and the specific way each one gets missed by a clean-looking automated scan.

learningObjectives.text: Apply 1.1.1, 1.3.1, 1.4.3, 1.4.11, and 2.1.1 to identify passes and failures in real markup
Distinguish an attribute's technical presence from a criterion's substantive requirement

contentSections.body: The automated scanner Havenmark's dev team already runs in CI reports zero errors on the homepage and the product listing pages. Your manual pass, an hour in, has found four real findings the scanner missed entirely — not because the scanner is broken, but because every one of them is a case where something is *technically present* — an alt attribute, a bold table cell, a grey that measures above zero contrast — without meeting what the actual success criterion requires. This is the shape of most real audit findings: not "missing," but "present and insufficient," which is exactly the category an automated tool structurally can't judge.

**1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A)** — every meaningful image needs a text alternative that serves the same purpose as the image; purely decorative images need `alt=""` so a screen reader skips them, rather than announcing a filename or nothing at all. Havenmark's product thumbnails have `alt="IMG_4471.jpg"` — an attribute is present, so an automated scanner marks it a pass, but it fails the actual criterion, because it conveys nothing a shopper could use to know what the photo shows. **1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)** — structure and relationships conveyed visually (headings, lists, table headers, required-field markers) also have to be programmatically determined, not just visually implied. Havenmark's size chart uses `Size` instead of a real `` with `scope` — visually it reads as a header row; structurally, a screen reader lands on a grid of numbers with no announced column meaning at all. **1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA)** — normal text needs at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio against its background; text at roughly 18pt (24px) or 14pt (18.66px) bold and larger — WCAG's definition of "large text" — only needs 3:1. Havenmark's price text, in the brand's grey `#767676` on white, comes out right around 4.54:1 — a genuine pass, and one of the most commonly cited "just clears it" greys in the field. The smaller `#999999` "Only 2 left in stock" urgency text, at normal size, sits well under 4.5:1 and fails outright. **1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (Level AA)** — the one most audits catch late: UI components (input borders, custom checkbox outlines, icon-only buttons) and graphical objects that convey meaning need 3:1 contrast against what's next to them, same threshold as large text. Havenmark's search input has a 1px border in a pale grey barely distinguishable from white — under 1.3:1 — so a low-vision user can't tell where the field boundary is, even though the placeholder text inside it separately passes 1.4.3 on its own. **2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A)** — every function has to be operable from a keyboard, with no interaction that depends on exact timing or a specific pointer path. The one narrow, genuine exception is a function whose *result* depends on the path of a user's movement — freehand drawing, not "we happened to build it as a slider." Havenmark's size-selector on product pages is a row of custom `
` swatches with click handlers and nothing else — no `keydown` handler, no `tabindex`. A keyboard user can't select a size at all, which doesn't just fail 2.1.1 in isolation — it means they can't complete a purchase.

contentSections.question: Havenmark's homepage banner has `alt="banner-hero-final-v3.jpg"`. Before you read on: does that count as a 1.1.1 pass, because an alt attribute is technically present?
contentSections.answer: No. 1.1.1 requires the alternative to serve the equivalent purpose of the image, not just exist as an attribute. A filename describes nothing about what's in the image, so this fails 1.1.1 even though an automated scanner sees a non-empty alt attribute and reports zero errors on it. The finding isn't "missing alt" — it's "meaningless alt," and most automated tools have no way to judge whether text is meaningful; they can only check whether the attribute exists.
contentSections.hint: Ask what the alt text is for, not whether one is present.

contentSections.question: This spec-sheet table visually reads as having a header row. What's the 1.3.1 finding?

options.label: The header row uses <td><b> instead of <th> with scope, so the row/column relationship is never programmatically determined
The table needs an aria-label naming what it's a table of
The table needs a <caption> element or it automatically fails 1.3.1

feedback.no-th-scope: Correct. Bold text visually simulates a header, but nothing in the markup tells the accessibility tree that "Size" and "Chest (cm)" are column headers rather than ordinary data. A screen reader user moving cell by cell hears "S," "92" with no announced header — the numbers are structurally meaningless out of context, which is exactly what 1.3.1 exists to prevent.
feedback.needs-aria-label: An aria-label would name the table as a whole ("Size chart"), which is a genuine improvement for orientation — but it does nothing to associate individual header cells with the data cells beneath them. The finding here is about cell-level relationships, not the table's overall name.
feedback.needs-caption: A caption is good practice for giving a table a visible, programmatically associated title, but WCAG doesn't require one for 1.3.1 to be met — a table can pass with correctly marked-up <th>/scope and no caption at all. Citing a missing caption as the 1.3.1 finding here names a nice-to-have, not the actual defect.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Bold text and table layout communicate structure visually. <th> (paired with scope="col" or scope="row" where the structure isn't obvious on its own) is what exposes that same structure to the accessibility tree. Without it, a sighted user and a screen reader user are reading two different tables from the same markup — one with headers, one without.

contentSections.scenario: Select every element on Havenmark's product page that has to clear 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — rather than, or in addition to, 1.4.3, which only applies to text.
contentSections.question: Which of these are 1.4.11 concerns?

items.label: The 1px border around the search input
A custom checkbox's outline when it's unchecked
An icon-only 'add to wishlist' heart button with no visible text label
The product price, rendered as text
A purely decorative background pattern behind the hero banner
The text inside a coloured 'Low stock' badge

explanation.search-border: Applicable. A form field's boundary is a UI component that a user has to be able to locate. 1.4.11 sets the 3:1 threshold for exactly this kind of non-text, functional element.
explanation.checkbox-outline: Applicable, for the same reason — the visual boundary of an interactive control has to be perceivable against its background, independent of whether the checkbox has an adjacent text label.
explanation.wishlist-icon: Applicable. Where an icon is the only way a control conveys its meaning (no visible text alongside it), the icon itself is the graphical object 1.4.11 is protecting.
explanation.price-text: Not applicable to 1.4.11 — it's text, so it's governed by 1.4.3 instead. The two criteria split cleanly on this line: text goes to 1.4.3, everything else visual and meaningful goes to 1.4.11.
explanation.decorative-pattern: Not applicable. Purely decorative content that conveys no information is exempt from contrast requirements entirely, the same way a decorative image is exempt from 1.1.1 — there's nothing for a low-vision user to fail to perceive, because the pattern isn't conveying anything.
explanation.stock-badge-text: Not applicable to 1.4.11 specifically — it's text inside the badge, so 1.4.3 covers it. The badge's background shape or border, if it's the only way the badge's boundary reads, would be a 1.4.11 question; the words inside it are not.

contentSections.synthesis: The split that matters: 1.4.3 is for text, 1.4.11 is for meaningful non-text — borders, icons, state indicators, graphical objects. Purely decorative elements are exempt from both. An audit that only runs a contrast checker against text is going to miss every non-text failure on the page, which is precisely why 1.4.11 is one of the most under-caught criteria in this list.

contentSections.body: Most real findings among these five criteria don't come from something being absent — they come from confusing an attribute's presence with a criterion being met: an alt that exists but says nothing, a bold cell that looks like a header but isn't one, a border with a colour value but not enough contrast to see. Test what's actually perceivable and operable, not what the markup technically contains.

title: Five Criteria, Part Two: Focus, Targets, Labels, and What a Screen Reader Can't Announce
description: 2.4.3, 2.4.7, 2.5.8, 3.3.2, and 4.1.2 — including a live disagreement in the field about how far focus-visibility findings should reach under WCAG 2.2.

learningObjectives.text: Apply 2.4.3, 2.4.7, 2.5.8, 3.3.2, and 4.1.2 to identify passes and failures in real interface patterns
Distinguish a criterion's literal wording from a related but distinct newer criterion covering similar territory

contentSections.body: Havenmark's checkout is where the second half of the audit's findings concentrate — not because checkout forms are unusually complex, but because focus order, focus visibility, target size, labelling, and custom widget behaviour all live exactly where a form has the most controls packed into the smallest space. A keyboard-only pass through the payment step alone turns up findings against five separate criteria before you reach the "Place order" button.

**2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A)** — where a page can be navigated sequentially, the order components receive focus has to preserve meaning and operability. Havenmark's order-summary panel is visually pinned to the right of the payment form with CSS, but written after the form in the DOM — a keyboard user tabs through every payment field before ever reaching "Edit cart," which sits right at the top of the screen.

**2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA)** — whenever a component receives keyboard focus, there has to be a visible indicator that it's focused. Havenmark's design system strips the default outline everywhere (`outline: none`) and re-adds a custom one selectively — but the payment-method radio buttons were missed, so tabbing through them shows nothing: no way to tell which option is currently focused. Worth being precise about this criterion's actual scope: 2.4.7 requires that an indicator *exists*. It does not, on its own wording, require that the indicator be unobscured by other content, or meet a stated size or contrast threshold — that's a separate, newer criterion, 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), added in WCAG 2.2 at Level AA, which this domain doesn't cover in full but which a current EU audit should increasingly be checking for too.

**2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA, new in WCAG 2.2)** — pointer targets need to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with four defined exceptions: the target sits inline within a sentence of text; its size is set by the user agent and unmodified by the author; an equivalent same-page control of adequate size achieves the same result; or the small size is essential to the information being conveyed. Havenmark's quantity-stepper minus/plus buttons are 16×16px icon buttons with no larger equivalent anywhere on the page — under the minimum, and none of the four exceptions apply.

**3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A)** — where input is required, a label or instructions must be provided. Havenmark's address form has a field with only a placeholder ("Apt, suite, etc.") and no `<label>` — placeholder text disappears the instant someone starts typing, and isn't reliably exposed as a label by every screen reader in every browser, so it doesn't satisfy 3.3.2 on its own.

**4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)** — every UI component needs a programmatically determined name and role, and, where applicable, its state has to be exposed and its state changes communicated to assistive technology. Havenmark's "Delivery country" selector is custom-built from styled `<div>` elements: it has no role, so a screen reader announces it as plain text with no indication it's interactive, and when a value is picked, nothing communicates the new state to assistive tech. This is the criterion most likely to mean rebuilding a component rather than patching it — a native `<select>` would have passed for free.

contentSections.question: Havenmark's minus/plus quantity buttons are 16×16px with no larger equivalent anywhere on the page. No mouse user has ever filed a complaint about them. Does the audit still have to cite 2.5.8?
contentSections.answer: Yes. 2.5.8 sets a measurable minimum with four named exceptions, and none of them apply here — the buttons aren't inline in text, their size isn't user-agent controlled, there's no adequately sized equivalent control, and small size isn't essential to what they convey. "Nobody's complained" isn't one of the exceptions, and it's exactly the kind of finding a mouse-only reviewer would never notice, since a mouse doesn't need 24 pixels of room to land precisely.
contentSections.hint: Check the finding against 2.5.8's own list of exceptions, not against whether anyone has raised a support ticket.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's sticky "Add to bag" bar sits fixed at the bottom of the viewport. A keyboard user tabs to a filter checkbox higher on the page; the browser's default focus ring appears around it, but at this scroll position the sticky bar visually covers the lower half of that same checkbox, hiding part of the ring.
contentSections.question: Does this pass 2.4.7 Focus Visible?

options.label: Yes, on 2.4.7's own wording — but it's a genuine candidate for 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, and whether that gets filed depends on which WCAG version the engagement was actually scoped against
No — a partly obscured indicator fails 2.4.7 outright
Yes, and there's nothing else worth noting here — one passing criterion covers this case

feedback.passes-2.4.7-flag-2.4.11: Correct — and this is a real, live judgment call, not a settled one. 2.4.7's text only requires that a keyboard-operable interface have a mode where the focus indicator is visible; it says nothing about obscuring. 2.4.11, added in WCAG 2.2, is what adds a requirement that the indicator not be entirely hidden by author-created content like a sticky footer. Whether a given engagement's scope — WCAG 2.1 AA versus 2.2 AA — actually obligates you to file this is a real difference in the field right now, and a scoping memo that names the WCAG edition up front is what settles it instead of leaving it to guesswork mid-audit.
feedback.fails-2.4.7-outright: This overstates what 2.4.7 checks. Its wording is about presence, not full unobstructed visibility — filing a partly obscured indicator as a 2.4.7 failure cites the wrong criterion, and a client's own accessibility lead checking the SC text against the finding will notice the mismatch, which costs the report credibility even when the underlying concern is legitimate.
feedback.nothing-to-flag: This under-reports a real, current problem. The user experience is genuinely degraded — half a focus ring is not a reliable way to track your position on a keyboard — even though the specific letter of 2.4.7 doesn't capture it. Stopping at "technically passes" misses exactly the kind of finding WCAG 2.2 was updated to catch.

contentSections.concept: New criteria get added to WCAG without rewriting the older ones they overlap with. 2.4.7 and 2.4.11 sit right next to each other and cover adjacent but distinct territory — this is a genuine area of live disagreement in the field about how audits should scope themselves as WCAG 2.2 becomes the default baseline, and the honest answer is: it depends on what standard and version the engagement was scoped against, stated explicitly, not assumed.

contentSections.scenario: Select every finding below that belongs under 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value — rather than one of the other criteria covered in this lesson.
contentSections.question: Which of these are 4.1.2 findings?

items.label: The custom country dropdown announces as plain text, with no indication it's interactive
A custom checkbox built from a styled <div>, with no role or checked state exposed
A live cart-count badge that updates visually but issues no notification to assistive tech when it changes
The quantity-stepper buttons are under 24x24 CSS pixels
The address field has only a placeholder and no <label>
The payment-method radio buttons show no focus ring when tabbed to

explanation.dropdown-no-role: Applicable. No role means assistive tech has no way to know this is an interactive control at all — squarely 4.1.2's territory.
explanation.checkbox-div-no-state: Applicable. Missing role and missing exposed state (checked/unchecked) are both exactly what 4.1.2 requires be programmatically available.
explanation.cart-badge-silent: Applicable. 4.1.2 covers notification of state changes to assistive tech, not just the initial name/role/value — a value that updates without any signal is a 4.1.2 gap even if the initial markup was fine.
explanation.stepper-small: Not applicable to 4.1.2 — this is a measurable size problem, which is 2.5.8's territory, not a naming or state-exposure problem.
explanation.placeholder-only: Not applicable to 4.1.2 — the input has a native role and state already (it's a real `<input>`); what it lacks is a label, which is 3.3.2's territory.
explanation.radio-no-outline: Not applicable to 4.1.2 — the radio buttons almost certainly have correct name, role, and state already; what's missing is a visible focus indicator, which is 2.4.7's territory.

contentSections.synthesis: 4.1.2 findings share a signature: something built from generic markup (a <div>, a <span>) standing in for a real interactive control, so the accessibility tree has no idea what it's looking at. The other three items in this set have working roles and states already — their problems are elsewhere, in size, labelling, or visual indication, which is exactly why filing a finding under the right criterion number matters: it tells the developer what actually needs to change.

contentSections.body: Focus order and focus visibility are related but distinct; a criterion's literal wording is what you cite, not the broader problem it's adjacent to. Target size is a measurable threshold with four named exceptions, not a judgment call about complaints. And a custom-built control with no role, name, or exposed state is the one finding in this list that usually means rebuilding, not patching.

title: EN 301 549: The Standard the Contract Actually Names
description: The European harmonised standard for ICT accessibility — how it incorporates WCAG by reference, and what it covers that WCAG never touches at all.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the relationship between EN 301 549 and WCAG success criteria
Identify what an EN 301 549 engagement scope includes beyond web content

contentSections.body: Havenmark's procurement and legal team sends over the signed statement of work, and it names "EN 301 549" — not WCAG. The account lead, who has spent three lessons learning WCAG success criteria in detail, asks the obvious question: is that a different standard, the same standard with a different name, or something in between? Getting this wrong in the scoping memo isn't a technicality — it's the difference between an audit that covers what the client's legal team actually needs and one that quietly leaves half of it out.

**What EN 301 549 is** — "Accessibility requirements for ICT products and services," a European Standard produced jointly by three European standards bodies (ETSI, CEN, and CENELEC). It's the standard EU public-procurement rules and the European Accessibility Act actually reference and grant presumption-of-conformity status to — WCAG is a W3C document; EN 301 549 is what the EU's legal and standards apparatus cites directly.

**How it relates to WCAG** — for web content specifically, EN 301 549 doesn't invent new criteria. Its web clause incorporates the WCAG success criteria by reference and restates them as normative requirements, largely following WCAG's own numbering. Practically, testing a page against EN 301 549's web clause and testing it against WCAG Level A/AA success criteria is the same technical work, presented under a different name for a different audience.

**Where it goes further than "web"** — this is the part a WCAG-only background misses entirely. EN 301 549 also has clauses for hardware (physical controls, ports, biometric input), non-web documents (PDFs, office files), software (native apps and platform software, not just what runs in a browser), and documentation and support services (user guides, help-desk interactions — the support itself has to be accessible, not just the product it supports). If Havenmark's audit scope stops at the website, it covers the web clause and misses whatever the hardware, document, software, and support clauses would apply to their in-store self-checkout kiosks, their mobile app, and their customer-service documentation.

**A version caveat worth stating plainly** — EN 301 549 has been revised multiple times since it was first published, and different revisions have referenced different editions of WCAG as the underlying technical baseline. Exactly which WCAG edition the current published version of EN 301 549 incorporates — and even the precise clause numbering, which has also shifted across revisions — isn't something to state from memory on a live engagement. It's exactly the kind of detail to confirm against the current published standard, and against whatever specific version the client's contract or the relevant Official Journal reference actually names, before a scoping memo goes out with a version number in it. Getting this wrong in a signed memo is a credibility problem, not a rounding error — which is also why this lesson states the relationship and the structure, and doesn't pin an exact version number to it.

contentSections.question: Havenmark's contract says: "the vendor shall conform to EN 301 549." Before you read on: does that mean something different from a contract that says "the vendor shall conform to WCAG 2.2 AA"?
contentSections.answer: For the web content itself, usually not much in substance — EN 301 549's web clause restates the WCAG Level A/AA success criteria. But "EN 301 549" as a whole is a broader ask than "WCAG": it can also reach the mobile app, PDFs and documents, self-service kiosks, and support services, none of which a WCAG-only clause would obviously cover. Reading "EN 301 549" and mentally substituting "WCAG" is a common scoping mistake — it under-scopes everything WCAG doesn't touch.
contentSections.hint: Ask what EN 301 549 covers that has no WCAG equivalent at all.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's RFP reads: "Audit us against EN 301 549 ahead of the EAA deadline." The agency proposes testing the marketing site and online store against WCAG 2.2 Level A/AA, and calling the engagement done.
contentSections.question: What does the proposed scope leave out that citing EN 301 549 — rather than WCAG — puts back on the table?

options.label: The self-checkout kiosks, the native mobile app, and support documentation, which fall under EN 301 549's hardware, software, and documentation clauses — none of which WCAG addresses at all
Nothing — EN 301 549's web clause and WCAG 2.2 A/AA test the same success criteria, so the proposal covers everything the client asked for
The proposal should test against WCAG AAA instead of AA, since EN 301 549 requires the higher level

feedback.kiosks-app-docs: Correct. The client asked to be tested against EN 301 549, the whole standard, not "EN 301 549's web clause." Havenmark's kiosks, app, and support documentation are exactly the kind of scope a WCAG-only proposal silently drops — and dropping them isn't a minor omission, since kiosks and native apps are named categories under the European Accessibility Act too.
feedback.nothing-left-out: This is technically accurate about the web clause specifically, and still the wrong conclusion. Being correct that clause 9 and WCAG 2.2 A/AA line up doesn't make the proposal complete, because the client's request was for EN 301 549 as a whole — an RFP naming the full standard is not satisfied by scoping only the part of it that happens to overlap with WCAG.
feedback.should-be-aaa: EN 301 549 references WCAG's Level A and AA success criteria, not AAA — this option gets the actual relationship backwards. The scoping gap here isn't about level; it's about which product categories and document types are in scope at all.

contentSections.mechanism: "EN 301 549" and "WCAG A/AA" overlap almost completely for web content and diverge completely everywhere else. A proposal that treats the two names as interchangeable is quietly scoping down from what the client's own language asked for — and the gap only shows up later, when someone asks why the kiosks were never tested.

contentSections.body: EN 301 549's web clause and WCAG Level A/AA are, for practical testing purposes, the same work under a different cover sheet — but EN 301 549 as a whole reaches hardware, non-web documents, software, and support services that WCAG never addresses. When a contract names EN 301 549, confirm the current version and clause numbering before the memo goes out, and scope for everything the standard actually covers, not just the part that happens to be a website.

title: The European Accessibility Act: Who It Binds, and the Exceptions That Get Abused
description: What the EAA covers, who it binds, the 2025 applicability date, the microenterprise exemption, and the disproportionate-burden claim — used legitimately, and used as a shortcut.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what products and services the EAA covers and which economic operators it binds
Evaluate whether a microenterprise exemption or disproportionate-burden claim is properly grounded or being used as a shortcut

contentSections.body: Havenmark's finance director asks two questions on the kickoff call, back to back: "Are we even covered by this law?" and, before you can fully answer the first, "Can we just claim it's too expensive to fix all of it?" Both are reasonable questions from someone who has heard of the European Accessibility Act secondhand and wants to know how much of this is actually mandatory. Both have real, specific answers — and both answers are narrower than the finance director is hoping.

**What the EAA is** — Directive (EU) 2019/882, the European Accessibility Act. As a directive, it didn't apply directly the way an EU regulation would; each member state had to transpose it into national law, by 28 June 2022. Its substantive obligations apply from **28 June 2025**, for products placed on the market and services provided from that date onward — a date that has now passed.

**What it covers** — a specific, listed set of products and services, not "digital accessibility" as a general concept: consumer computer hardware and operating systems; self-service terminals (ATMs, ticketing and check-in machines); consumer terminal equipment for electronic communications (phones) and for accessing audiovisual media; e-readers; electronic communications services; audiovisual media access services; the parts of air, bus, rail, and waterborne passenger transport that are digital (websites, apps, e-ticketing, real-time travel information); consumer banking services; e-books; and **e-commerce**. Havenmark is in scope specifically because it sells to consumers online — its website and checkout are e-commerce under the EAA. The Act is what creates the legal obligation; EN 301 549 and WCAG are what define what meeting it actually looks like.

**Who it binds** — "economic operators": manufacturers, importers, and distributors of covered products, and providers of covered services, where they're established in the EU or place products or provide services into the EU market, for EU consumers. A mid-size EU retailer selling into the EU market, like Havenmark, sits squarely inside that definition.

**The microenterprise exemption — narrower than it sounds** — Article 4(5) exempts **microenterprises providing services** (fewer than 10 employees, and either annual turnover or annual balance-sheet total no more than €2 million — the standard EU microenterprise test) from the EAA's accessibility requirements entirely, for the services they provide. Two details matter for scoping: both the headcount test and one of the two financial thresholds have to actually hold, and the exemption applies to *service* providers specifically — a microenterprise that manufactures or imports a covered *product* doesn't get this blanket exemption, though it can still raise disproportionate burden case by case like any other operator. Havenmark, as a mid-size retailer, doesn't come close to either threshold, so this exemption simply isn't available to it — but the precision matters, because "we're basically a small operation" is a feeling, and the exemption is a defined test with two numbers in it.

**Disproportionate burden — legitimate use, and the abuse of it** — Article 14 lets an economic operator claim an exception where meeting a requirement would impose a disproportionate burden, or require a fundamental alteration to the product or service. This has to be assessed against defined criteria in Annex VI: the ratio of compliance cost to the operator's overall costs; the estimated cost weighed against the benefit to people with disabilities, considering how often and how long the product or service is used; and the ratio of compliance cost to net turnover. **Used legitimately**, this looks like a documented assessment against those specific criteria, applied to the specific requirement that's genuinely disproportionate rather than a blanket opt-out from the whole engagement, kept on file, and revisited when the product or the company's circumstances change. **Used as an abuse**, it looks like an unsupported claim that something is "too expensive," with no documented cost analysis at all; invoking it for an entire engagement rather than the specific line items that are actually disproportionate; treating cost in isolation without ever weighing it against user benefit, which the assessment is explicitly required to include; or a claim made once and never revisited against a product that has since changed substantially. An audit that accepts a disproportionate-burden claim at face value, without asking to see the documented assessment behind it, isn't doing the job the claim's own legal basis assumes it will do.

**Enforcement — deliberately not a number** — the EAA requires member states to designate market-surveillance authorities and to set penalties that are "effective, proportionate and dissuasive," but leaves the actual penalty regime to each member state's own transposing law. There's real variation across the EU in what enforcement looks like in practice, and a good deal of it is genuinely untested at this point. Stating a specific fine figure as though it were one EU-wide fact would be wrong regardless of which number got picked. What's stable across the EU is the applicability date and the listed scope; what isn't is the exact consequence of non-compliance in any one member state — and a scoping memo should say so, rather than invent a number to sound more authoritative than the law actually is.

contentSections.question: Havenmark's finance director wants to invoke disproportionate burden to skip fixing the checkout's keyboard trap, citing "it would cost too much to rebuild before the deadline." Before you answer: is a cost estimate alone enough to make this a valid Article 14 claim?
contentSections.answer: No. Annex VI's criteria weigh cost against benefit to users and against the operator's overall costs and turnover — not cost by itself. A number with no comparison to those isn't an assessment, it's an assertion. And even a properly documented claim would only exempt the specific requirement it was assessed against — it wouldn't retroactively cover the rest of the audit's findings, and it wouldn't apply to a barrier that blocks a purchase outright, which is exactly the kind of high-user-impact finding Annex VI's cost-benefit criterion weighs hardest against.
contentSections.hint: Check what Annex VI actually asks the assessment to compare cost against.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's finance team sends over a one-paragraph note justifying skipping three of the audit's findings, citing disproportionate burden. Select every element that would actually be present in a claim that holds up to scrutiny.
contentSections.question: Which of these belong in a defensible disproportionate-burden claim?

items.label: A documented cost estimate specific to the finding it's attached to, not a total for the whole project
A comparison of that cost against the estimated benefit to affected users, considering how often the feature is used
A statement that the claim will be reassessed if the product or the company's circumstances change
The claim is scoped to one specific requirement, leaving the rest of the audit's findings in scope for remediation
A round number described as 'too expensive for a company our size,' with no supporting detail
No written analysis at all, because the finance director is confident it would be uneconomical

explanation.specific-cost: Belongs. Annex VI's criteria are about the cost of the specific requirement being exempted, not a blended estimate for everything the audit found — a claim covering three unrelated findings under one number can't actually be tested against any of the criteria.
explanation.cost-vs-benefit: Belongs. This is the criterion most abused claims skip entirely — cost in isolation isn't what Annex VI asks for; it's cost weighed against user benefit, which requires actually estimating how many people are affected and how often.
explanation.reassess-trigger: Belongs. A disproportionate-burden claim isn't permanent — the underlying facts (company size, product changes, cost of remediation as tooling improves) shift, and a claim with no reassessment trigger is functionally a claim nobody intends to revisit.
explanation.narrow-scope: Belongs. The claim's whole legal basis is that a specific requirement is disproportionate — extending that finding to justify leaving unrelated findings unaddressed goes beyond what Article 14 actually authorizes.
explanation.round-number: Doesn't belong. 'Too expensive for a company our size' with no cost breakdown and no comparison to benefit isn't an assessment against Annex VI's criteria — it's a business preference stated in the language of a legal exception.
explanation.no-analysis: Doesn't belong. Confidence is not documentation. Article 14's exception exists on the condition that the burden is actually assessed against defined criteria — skipping the assessment isn't a shortcut to the exception, it's the thing that makes the claim invalid on its face.

contentSections.synthesis: The four that belong all point at the same underlying requirement: a disproportionate-burden claim is a documented, narrow, revisitable analysis, not a business decision dressed up in the language of a legal exception. The two that don't belong are the shape the abuse usually takes — confident, unsupported, and broader than the specific thing it's supposedly justifying.

contentSections.body: EAA scope is a specific, listed set of products and services — not a general vibe about "digital accessibility." The microenterprise exemption is a two-part headcount-and-turnover test, and it applies to service providers. Disproportionate burden is a documented, narrow, revisitable claim measured against defined criteria, not a shortcut for "we'd rather not." And enforcement specifics vary by member state — a scoping memo names the applicability date and the scope with confidence, and names the penalty question as genuinely open.

title: Writing the Conformance Scoping Memo
description: Producing the domain artefact: the memo that states, before any testing starts, what standard, what level, which pages and processes, what's excluded and why, and what exceptions — if any — are being claimed.

learningObjectives.text: Draft a conformance scoping memo that names standard, level, in-scope pages and processes, exclusions, and exception claims
Evaluate a scoping memo or accessibility statement against a rubric for completeness and honesty about what was and wasn't tested

contentSections.body: Havenmark's kickoff is done. Everyone in the room — the project sponsor, the finance director, the dev lead — has heard the standards, the levels, and the exceptions explained across the last five lessons. Before a single test runs, one document has to exist and be signed off: the conformance scoping memo. It's the artefact that turns everything covered so far — WCAG's structure, EN 301 549's reach, the EAA's scope and its exceptions — into a specific, written, defensible statement of exactly what this audit will and won't cover, and why.

**Accessibility statements — what belongs in one.** A compliant accessibility statement — the model most clearly established for public-sector bodies under the EU's Web Accessibility Directive, and one that private-sector companies increasingly mirror as standard practice even where the EAA doesn't spell out an identically codified statement obligation for every covered service — states, at minimum: the exact scope it covers (which site, app, or named set of pages, and as of what date); the standard and level being claimed (e.g. "WCAG 2.2 Level AA"); how conformance was assessed (self-assessment, third-party audit, or a mix, and when); every known non-conformance, named specifically, with the reason it exists; a real feedback mechanism — a contact route for someone who hits a barrier, ideally with an expected response time; and the date the statement was last reviewed. It's worth being precise about where that list comes from: the clearest, most codified legal duty to publish a statement in that exact shape sits with public-sector bodies. Whether a specific private-sector service falls under an identical, EU-wide statement mandate under the EAA is more a matter of national transposition and sector rules than one clean answer — which is exactly the kind of detail to verify against Havenmark's specific situation rather than assume from the public-sector model.

**The scoping memo — what it has to answer, in writing, before testing starts.** A conformance scoping memo names: **which standard** (WCAG 2.2, EN 301 549, or a client-specified combination — and if EN 301 549, which of its clauses beyond the web one, per the standard's reach); **which level**, named explicitly rather than left implicit, almost always AA; **which pages and processes** are in scope, listed or defined by an unambiguous rule — never "the whole site"; **what's explicitly excluded, and why** — a legacy microsite scheduled for decommission, third-party embedded widgets outside the client's control, PDF documents on a separate remediation track; and **any EAA exception being claimed** — disproportionate burden, microenterprise status — stated with its documented basis, not asserted. A memo that skips the exclusions section isn't more thorough for leaving it out — it's setting up a dispute later about what the audit was ever supposed to cover.

contentSections.question: Havenmark's marketing team asks why the memo needs an "excluded" section at all — wouldn't it read stronger to just say the audit covers "the whole site"?
contentSections.answer: No — "the whole site" isn't a testable scope, and it invites exactly the dispute an exclusions section prevents: months later, someone finds a page nobody actually tested and calls it a broken promise. Naming what's out, and why, is what makes the "in" list mean something specific and checkable.
contentSections.hint: Ask what happens later when someone finds a page nobody actually looked at.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the four load-bearing fields of Havenmark's scoping memo. One decision at a time.

fields.prompt: Which standard does the memo name, given this engagement is web-only?

options.label: WCAG 2.2 Level AA, noted as satisfying EN 301 549's web clause — with clauses on hardware, documents, software, and support explicitly out of scope
EN 301 549, unqualified
WCAG 2.2 Level AAA, to be safe

feedback.wcag22-aa-mapped-to-en301549-web-clause-: Right. This names the actual standard being tested against, states plainly what it satisfies, and closes off the exact scoping trap from the EN 301 549 lesson — nobody reading this memo can mistake it for covering the kiosks or the app.
feedback.en301549-unqualified: This is precisely the trap this domain flagged earlier: naming the whole standard without saying which clauses apply implies a scope — hardware, documents, software — that a web-only engagement was never going to cover. It reads as a bigger promise than the work.
feedback.wcag22-aaa: AAA was never the target — WCAG's own guidance advises against requiring it site-wide, and no EU standard or law references it as a baseline. This sounds rigorous and states the wrong level entirely.

fields.prompt: How should in-scope pages and processes be listed?

options.label: A named list of URL patterns and processes (e.g. product pages, the three-step checkout, account creation)
A count of pages tested (e.g. '50 pages')
Whatever pages the automated scanner could crawl in the time available

feedback.named-list-of-pages-and-processes: Right. A named list — including the checkout as a process, not just a page — is the only version someone can check the memo against after the fact and know whether a given page or flow was actually covered.
feedback.page-count: A count tells you volume, not which pages. "50 pages" gives Havenmark's team nothing to check a specific URL against, and it can't distinguish tested pages from untested ones with any precision.
feedback.scanner-crawl-reach: This describes a tooling limitation, not a scoping decision — and it silently excludes anything behind a login (like the account area) without ever saying so, which is exactly the kind of quiet gap a scoping memo exists to prevent.

fields.prompt: What's the right way to handle the legacy PDF product catalogue, which is out of scope for this engagement?

options.label: Name it specifically and state the reason: 'Excluded — scheduled for a separate remediation track'
Leave it out of the memo entirely, since it isn't part of this engagement
List it as 'in scope, pending' without committing to an answer

feedback.named-with-reason: Right. This is the exclusions section doing its job — anyone reading the memo knows the catalogue exists, was considered, and was deliberately routed elsewhere, rather than simply forgotten.
feedback.silent-omission: This is the exact dispute this lesson opened with, just in miniature: months from now, someone finds the catalogue, finds no mention of it anywhere, and reasonably assumes it was missed rather than deliberately excluded.
feedback.ambiguous-pending: 'Pending' isn't a scoping decision — it commits to nothing and leaves the reader unable to tell whether the catalogue is in this engagement's remit or a future one.

fields.prompt: Havenmark hasn't made any EAA exception claims for this engagement. What goes in that section of the memo?

options.label: An explicit statement: 'No EAA exceptions (disproportionate burden or microenterprise status) are claimed for this engagement'
Nothing — omit the section, since there's nothing to say
A placeholder noting disproportionate burden 'may apply to some findings,' without specifics

feedback.explicit-none-claimed: Right. An explicit 'none claimed' is a checkable statement — if a finding shows up later with an unsupported cost objection attached, the memo already establishes that no exception was on the table when scope was agreed.
feedback.omit-section: Omitting the section is indistinguishable, to a later reader, from forgetting to check whether any exceptions applied. The whole value of naming this explicitly is that it can't be read either way.
feedback.vague-hedge: This is the abuse pattern from the previous lesson, pre-loaded into the memo itself — a vague 'may apply' with no documented Annex VI analysis behind it isn't a real claim, and it leaves the door open to invoking it later without ever having actually assessed it.

contentSections.synthesis: Standard, scope, exclusions, exceptions — named specifically, in writing, before testing starts. Every one of these four fields is where a vague version reads as more generous and a specific version is the only one that actually protects both sides of the engagement later.

contentSections.body:
**The brief.** Havenmark's project sponsor has asked for a one-page memo, addressed to their legal and procurement team, that can be attached to the audit's statement of work: what standard and level the audit tests against, which pages and processes are in scope, what's explicitly excluded and why, and whether any EAA exceptions are being claimed. It has to be readable by someone with no accessibility background, precise enough that a developer can act on it, and honest about its own limits.

**The rubric.** A memo that clears the bar: (1) names the standard and level explicitly — no bare "WCAG compliant"; (2) if EN 301 549 is referenced, states which of its clauses apply to this engagement, not just the web one; (3) lists in-scope pages and processes concretely, including any multi-step process by name; (4) lists exclusions by name, each with a stated reason; (5) states plainly whether any EAA exception is being claimed, and if so, on what documented basis; (6) is dated, and states what happens if scope needs to change mid-engagement. A memo that hits five of six is missing the sixth for a reason worth asking about — not a rounding error.

**Worked exemplar.**

> **Havenmark — Accessibility Conformance Scoping Memo**
> *Prepared [date]. Applies to the engagement described in the attached statement of work.*
>
> **Standard and level:** WCAG 2.2 Level AA (all Level A and Level AA success criteria). This satisfies EN 301 549's web clause (9) as referenced in the EAA. Clauses covering hardware, non-web documents, native software, and support services are **not** included in this engagement and would require a separate scope.
>
> **In scope:** the havenmark.eu marketing site and online store, specifically: all product listing and product detail pages; the three-step checkout process (cart → shipping and payment → confirmation) tested end to end as a single process, not as isolated pages; account creation and login; and the customer-support contact form.
>
> **Excluded, with reason:** the legacy PDF product catalogue (600+ files) — routed to a separate remediation track, scoped once this audit's web findings are delivered; the in-store self-checkout kiosks and the native mobile app — out of scope for this engagement, and flagged to Havenmark's team as requiring separate EN 301 549 hardware- and software-clause coverage; third-party embedded payment widgets — tested for keyboard operability and labelling only, since Havenmark does not control their underlying markup.
>
> **EAA exceptions claimed:** none. Havenmark does not meet the microenterprise threshold (Article 4(5)), and no disproportionate-burden assessment under Article 14 has been requested or prepared for any finding in this engagement's scope.
>
> **Change control:** any change to the above scope will be documented in a dated revision to this memo before affected testing begins.

The scoping memo is the artefact everything else in this domain was building toward: a standard and level named without hedging, a scope specific enough to check against later, exclusions named rather than silently dropped, and exception claims stated as explicitly absent rather than left ambiguous. Everything downstream — the audit itself, the remediation tickets, the accessibility statement — inherits whatever this document got vague about.
